events.title: Neolithic Vinča Culture
events.description: Advanced Neolithic cultures emerged in Serbian territory, particularly Vinča culture, one of Europe's most important prehistoric cultures. Vinča site located near Belgrade on Danube River, famous for pottery, figurines, copper work and possible proto-writing system (Vinča script). Vinča culture showed highly developed social organization and trade networks, influencing entire Balkan region. Archaeological discoveries include complex settlements, religious idols and early metalworking evidence.

events.title: Celtic and Thracian-Illyrian Tribes
events.description: Serbian territory inhabited by multiple tribes: Triballi in north, Scordisci (Celtic tribe), Dardani and Moesi in south. Tribes built fortified towns, engaged in agriculture and trade. Celtic Scordisci established Singidunum settlement (Belgrade area). Tribes clashed with Macedonian Kingdom and later Roman Republic. Tribal society characterized by warrior culture, metalwork and trade with Greek world.

events.title: Roman Conquest Begins
events.description: Roman Republic began conquering Balkans after Third Macedonian War. Roman legions fought local Illyrian and Thracian tribes, gradually expanding control. Conquest difficult, local tribes resisted fiercely. Romans established military posts and road networks, beginning Romanization process. This marked Serbian territory entering Roman sphere, laying foundation for centuries of Roman rule.

events.title: Moesia Province Established
events.description: Emperor Augustus completed conquest, establishing Moesia province covering most of modern Serbia. Later Moesia divided into Moesia Superior (including Serbia) and Moesia Inferior. Province bordered Danube River as northern frontier, becoming important Roman border defending against barbarian invasions. Romans built numerous cities, fortresses, roads and bridges. Province underwent rapid Romanization, adopting Latin language, Roman law and lifestyle. Moesia became important military zone with multiple legions stationed.

events.title: Roman Prosperity Period
events.description: Serbian territory prospered under Roman rule. Important cities included: Singidunum (Belgrade), Viminacium (Moesia Superior capital), Sirmium (later capital), Naissus (Niš). Extensive road network built connecting Danube to Adriatic and Aegean Seas. Region produced grain, wine, minerals and hosted large armies. Many Roman emperors born here including Constantine the Great. Cities had theaters, baths, forums and temples. Archaeological sites like Felix Romuliana showcase Roman cultural brilliance.

events.title: Sirmium: Imperial Capital
events.description: Sirmium (modern Sremska Mitrovica) became one of Rome's most important cities, called 'Glorious Mother Sirmium' (Mater Sirmium gloriosa). City located on Sava River, strategic position and trade center. Sirmium repeatedly served as Roman emperors' residence, including Marcus Aurelius during Marcomannic Wars. Under Diocletian's Tetrarchy, Sirmium became one of four imperial capitals, ruling Balkan region. City had imperial palace, hippodrome, baths, mint and large Christian community. Multiple emperors and Caesars resided and ruled here. Sirmium's brilliance demonstrated Serbian territory's core position in Late Roman period, until destroyed by barbarians.

events.title: Barbarian Invasions and Roman Decline
events.description: Serbian region suffered continuous barbarian invasions: Goths, Huns, Avars. After Battle of Adrianople 378, Goths ravaged Balkans. 5th century Huns invaded under Attila. Roman cities sacked, population declined, economy collapsed. Byzantine Empire (Eastern Rome) tried maintaining control but struggled. Urban defenses strengthened but many Roman settlements abandoned. This marked decline of classical civilization and beginning of chaotic period. Byzantine Emperor Justinian I (527-565) briefly restored parts, rebuilding cities and fortresses, but invasions continued.

events.title: April War and Yugoslav Surrender
events.description: Nazi Germany and allies (Italy, Hungary, Bulgaria) invaded Yugoslavia. April 6, German Luftwaffe bombed Belgrade without warning, causing massive civilian casualties, operation code-named "Punishment." Yugoslav army rapidly collapsed, partly due to internal ethnic divisions, many Croatian and Slovenian units refused fighting. April 17 Yugoslavia surrendered, royal family and government exiled to London. State partitioned: Germany occupied Serbia, Italy occupied Montenegro and Kosovo, Bulgaria occupied Macedonia, Hungary occupied Vojvodina. Independent State of Croatia (NDH) established, ruled by Ustaša fascist regime. Yugoslav Kingdom perished. Serbian homeland under German military occupation and puppet government (Milan Nedić regime), beginning four years of suffering, resistance and civil war.

events.title: Great Slavic Migration
events.description: Slavic tribes began massive migration into Balkan Peninsula, settling Serbian territory. Slavs came from north of Carpathian Mountains, pushed south by Avars. They settled river valleys and plains, engaging in agriculture. Slavic migration permanently changed Balkan demographics, Roman-Illyrian population assimilated or migrated. Serbs (Srbi) were one South Slavic tribe, related to Croats, Slovenes. Slavs brought own language (Slavic), religion (pagan polytheism) and social organization (tribal clan system). Byzantine sources first mentioned Serbs around 7th century.

events.title: Early Serbian Tribal States
events.description: Serbs established multiple tribal principalities (župas) ruled by Grand Župan (veliki župan). Main principalities included Raška (core region), Duklja (later Zeta/Montenegro), Travunija and Zahumlje. These principalities existed between Byzantine, First Bulgarian Empire and Frankish Empire influence, often in vassal status. Serbs gradually accepted Christian influence, though full Christianization came in 9th century. Early Serbian rulers included Višeslav, leaving inscriptions. Society based on agriculture, pastoralism and clan system.

events.title: Byzantine and Bulgarian Contest
events.description: Serbian principalities oscillated between Byzantine Empire and Bulgarian Empire, often in vassal status. Bulgarian Tsar Simeon I conquered most Serbian territory, forcing submission. After Byzantine Emperor Basil II ("Bulgar-Slayer") destroyed Bulgarian Empire in 1018, Serbia returned to Byzantine rule. Byzantium established themes (military administrative districts) in Serbia, but local župans maintained considerable autonomy. Serbian culture strongly influenced by Byzantium, church organization and art style imitated Constantinople. Duklja principality maintained relative independence at times, even gaining royal title.

events.title: Birth of Emperor Probus
events.description: Roman Emperor Marcus Aurelius Probus born in Sirmium (modern Sremska Mitrovica). Probus ruled Roman Empire 276-282, capable military commander and reformer. He defeated Germanic invaders, consolidated borders, promoted agriculture (allowing provinces to cultivate vineyards), conducted military and administrative reforms. Probus was one of Illyrian Emperors who saved Roman Empire during 3rd century crisis. Serbian territory became cradle of Roman military elite, producing multiple emperors and generals, demonstrating region's importance in Empire.

events.title: Birth of Diocletian the Great
events.description: Gaius Aurelius Valerius Diocletianus (Diocletian) possibly born in Dalmatia (near modern Serbian territory), later becoming one of Rome's greatest reformers. Diocletian ruled 284-305, established Tetrarchy (four emperors ruling together), thoroughly reformed Empire's administrative, military and economic systems, ending 3rd century crisis. He divided Empire into Eastern and Western parts, established new capitals (including Nicomedia), strengthened defenses, issued price edicts. Sirmium became one of four Tetrarchic capitals. Diocletian's reforms laid foundation for Constantine and later Byzantine Empire. He was last emperor to launch major Christian persecution, but also stabilized Empire. Serbian territory reached peak political importance in Diocletian's era.

events.title: Birth of Constantine the Great
events.description: Constantine I (Constantine the Great) born in Naissus (Niš), later becoming one of Rome's most important emperors. Constantine legalized Christianity (Edict of Milan, 313), founded Constantinople as new capital, unified Roman Empire. His birthplace Niš became historically significant. Constantine's connection with Serbian territory gave region special place in Roman Imperial history. Niš preserves Constantine-era remains including Mediana villa site. Constantine the Great considered important figure in Serbian history.

events.title: Edict of Milan and Legalization of Christianity
events.description: Constantine the Great (born in Serbian Niš) met with Licinius in Milan, issued Edict of Milan proclaiming religious tolerance, ending Christian persecution. This was world history turning point: Christianity transformed from persecuted religion to legal religion, eventually becoming Roman state religion. Serbian territory's Christian communities were quite active in Roman period, cities like Niš and Sirmium were early Christian centers with bishops and martyrs. Edict of Milan opened Christianity's triumph in Europe, and this key decision made by emperor born in Serbia. Constantine later founded Constantinople, shifting Empire's center eastward, crucial for Balkans' future history (Byzantine civilization). Serbia thus deeply connected with Christian history.

events.title: Christianization
events.description: Serbs officially accepted Christianity, mainly under Byzantine influence. Byzantine missionaries spread Eastern Orthodoxy from east, while Roman Catholic influence came from western Dalmatia and Croatia. Most Serbian territory accepted Orthodox Christianity, connecting with Byzantine Church. Christianization brought literacy (Glagolitic and later Cyrillic alphabet), Byzantine culture and new social organization. Ruler Mutimir's reign saw Serbia establish Orthodox faith. Church established monasteries and churches, becoming cultural and educational centers. Christianization was crucial moment in Serbian nation formation, integrating with Byzantine civilization.

events.title: Reign of Grand Prince Časlav
events.description: Časlav Klonimirović obtained Raška region from Bulgaria, united multiple Serbian tribal principalities, establishing powerful Serbian state. Časlav considered one of greatest early Serbian rulers, expanded territory to Bosnia, Travunija and Zahumlje, building alliance from Sava River to Adriatic Sea. He maintained friendly relations with Byzantine Emperor, gaining recognition and support. Časlav promoted Christianization, strengthening church organization. He died in 960 fighting Magyars (Hungarians), after which Serbia fragmented again until Nemanjić unification. Časlav's reign was glorious moment in early Serbian history, demonstrating unification and expansion potential.

events.title: King Michael of Duklja
events.description: Duklja ruler Mihajlo (Michael Vojislavljević) received royal title from Pope Gregory VII, establishing "King of Slavs" (Rex Slavorum) title. This was first international recognition of Serbian royal authority. Duklja Kingdom briefly prospered, controlling Adriatic coastal areas and parts of interior. But kingdom declined in 12th century, internal divisions and Byzantine pressure led to its eclipse by Raška principality. Duklja's royal tradition and Rome connection left important legacy in Serbian history, later Serbian rulers claimed this inheritance.

events.title: Nemanjić Dynasty Founded
events.description: Stefan Nemanja became Grand Župan of Raška, founding Nemanjić dynasty ruling Serbia for nearly two centuries. Nemanja unified Serbian principalities, expanded territory, broke free from Byzantine control, establishing powerful medieval Serbian state. He defeated Byzantine armies, conquered Kosovo, Metohija and parts of Macedonia. Nemanja promoted Orthodoxy, built monasteries (like Studenica), establishing close Church-State ties. 1196 Nemanja abdicated, became monk, went to Mount Athos, took name Saint Simeon. Nemanja canonized by Serbian Orthodox Church, becoming national hero and father-figure. Nemanjić dynasty establishment was foundation of medieval Serbian statehood.

events.title: Kingdom of Serbia Established
events.description: Stefan Nemanja's son Stefan (Stefan Prvovenčani, "First-Crowned") received crown from Pope, establishing Kingdom of Serbia. Stefan's coronation as king marked Serbia's elevation from principality to kingdom, gaining international recognition. Kingdom maintained Orthodox faith despite crown from Rome. Stefan balanced Eastern and Western Churches, consolidating royal power. He established Serbian medieval state institutional foundations: administrative system, currency, law. Serbian Kingdom became important Balkan power, interacting with Hungary, Venice, Byzantium and Bulgaria. Kingdom period marked beginning of Serbian medieval cultural flourishing.

events.title: Autocephalous Serbian Church Established
events.description: Saint Sava (Nemanja's youngest son, originally Rastko) obtained autocephalous status for Serbian Orthodox Church from Byzantine Nicaean Empire. Sava became first Serbian Archbishop, establishing church organization, dioceses and monastery network. Autocephalous church gave Serbia religious independence, breaking from Greek church control, using Slavic language in services. Saint Sava compiled church law (Nomocanon), organized education and cultural activities, considered founder of Serbian education and literature. Sava died 1235, later canonized, becoming Serbia's most revered saint, symbol of culture, education and national identity. January 27 is Saint Sava Day, important Serbian holiday.

events.title: Reign of King Milutin
events.description: Stefan Uroš II Milutin's reign was one of medieval Serbia's most glorious periods. Milutin greatly expanded territory, conquering most of Macedonia including Skopje, pushing south near Thessaloniki. He married Byzantine princess Simonida, strengthening Constantinople relations. Milutin was great builder, constructing over 40 churches and monasteries including masterpieces Gračanica and Stara Ravar, showcasing Serbian-Byzantine art peak. His court was cultural center, attracting artists, scholars and craftsmen. Milutin's reign consolidated Serbia as major Balkan power, laying foundation for later imperial expansion.

events.title: Serbian Cultural Golden Age
events.description: Under Nemanjić dynasty, Serbia experienced cultural flourishing. Numerous Raška-style monasteries and churches built: Studenica, Žiča, Sopoćani, Mileševa, featuring exquisite Byzantine-style frescoes. These frescoes are Byzantine art masterpieces, depicting biblical scenes, saints and Serbian rulers. Literature developed, writing religious and historical texts in Slavic (Old Serbian). Monasteries became manuscript copying centers, preserving ancient texts. Law codified, economy developed, mining (silver, gold, copper) prospered, trade with Venice, Ragusa (Dubrovnik) flourished. Serbian medieval culture combined Byzantine tradition with native Slavic characteristics, creating unique civilization.

events.title: Stefan Dušan Ascends
events.description: Stefan Dušan, son of Stefan Uroš III, overthrew his father through coup, becoming Serbian King. Dušan was ambitious, aiming to build Balkan empire and even conquer Constantinople. He was medieval Serbia's greatest ruler, elevating Serbia to unprecedented power and territorial peak. Dušan was outstanding military leader and strategist, also cultural patron and legislator. His ascension marked beginning of Serbian expansion era, transforming kingdom into empire under his rule.

events.title: Serbian Empire Proclaimed
events.description: Stefan Dušan crowned himself "Emperor of Serbs and Greeks" in Skopje, establishing Serbian Empire. Serbian Archbishop elevated to Patriarch, church equal with Constantinople. Dušan's imperial title challenged Byzantine Emperor's uniqueness, showing his ambition for Byzantine throne. Coronation held in Peć, combining Byzantine and Serbian traditions. Serbian Empire reached maximum territory, ruling Serbia, Macedonia, Albania, Thessaly and most of Epirus, stretching from Danube to Gulf of Corinth, from Adriatic to Aegean Seas. This was Serbian history's zenith, often called "Dušan's Empire."

events.title: Dušan's Code
events.description: Emperor Dušan promulgated comprehensive law code (Dušanov zakonik), becoming medieval Serbia's most important legal document. Code contained 201 articles covering church law, criminal law, civil law, property law, commercial law. Code based on Byzantine law, customary law and Serbian tradition, written in Slavic. It regulated social hierarchy (nobility, freemen, serfs), Church-State relations, judicial procedures. Dušan's Code showed highly developed legal system and state administration, considered one of medieval Balkans' most advanced laws. Code manuscripts preserved today, key source for studying medieval Serbian society. Code embodied Dušan's effort transforming empire into ordered, centralized state.

events.title: Dušan's Death and Empire Disintegration
events.description: Stefan Dušan died suddenly age 47 while preparing to march on Constantinople, possibly from illness or poisoning. His death was turning point in Serbian history. Successor was weak son Uroš V, unable to maintain empire unity. Powerful regional nobles (magnates, despots) declared independence, establishing own domains. Empire rapidly fragmented into competing principalities: Lazar Hrebeljanović's Moravian Serbia, Vukašin and Marko's Macedonian domains, Balšić family's Zeta. Fragmentation left Serbia vulnerable as Ottoman Empire rose, paving way for later conquest. Dušan Empire's brevity became Serbian history's tragedy, "if Dušan lived longer" becoming eternal hypothesis.

events.title: Battle of Maritsa
events.description: Serbian nobles Vukašin Mrnjavčević and Jovan Uglješa led army against Ottoman Turkish forces at Maritsa River (modern Bulgaria). Serbian army ambushed at night, suffered catastrophic defeat, both leaders killed. Maritsa was Serbia's first major defeat against Ottoman expansion, Ottomans gained control over most of Macedonia. After defeat, many Serbian lords forced to submit to Sultan Murad I as vassals. Battle celebrated in Serbian epic poetry, described as catastrophic event, foreshadowing Ottoman conquest. After Maritsa, Serbia fell into deeper fragmentation, unable to coordinate unified resistance against Ottoman threat.

events.title: Battle of Kosovo
events.description: Serbian Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović led Serbian, Bosnian and other Balkan allies against Ottoman Sultan Murad I's army at Kosovo Polje (Kosovo Field). Both sides suffered heavy losses: Lazar captured and executed, Murad assassinated by Serbian knight Miloš Obilić. Battle outcome disputed, but strategically Ottoman victory as Serbia lost independence, Lazar's successors became Ottoman vassals. Kosovo Battle occupies central place in Serbian history and national consciousness, viewed as national tragedy and sacrifice symbol. Lazar canonized as martyr saint. Battle date (Vidovdan, June 28) became Serbia's most important national commemoration day. Kosovo myth repeatedly appears in Serbian culture, epic poetry, art, shaping national identity to this day. Battle marked end of medieval Serbian independent statehood.

events.title: Stefan Lazarević Despot
events.description: Stefan Lazarević, Prince Lazar's son, ruled Serbian Despotate. Though nominally Ottoman vassal, Stefan was capable ruler, consolidating Serbia during Ottoman civil war after Battle of Ankara (1402). He moved capital to Belgrade, rebuilding city as powerful fortress. Stefan was cultural patron, court attracted scholars, poets and artists. He himself was poet and writer, works like "Praise of Kosovo Battle" showed literary talent. Stefan received Despot title from Hungarian King, elevating status. His reign was last cultural flourishing of Serbian culture before Ottoman conquest, called "Serbian Renaissance." Belgrade became important Balkan cultural center.

events.title: Fall of Serbian Despotate
events.description: Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II (the Conqueror) conquered last remnants of Serbian Despotate. Capital Smederevo surrendered after brief siege. Serbia lost statehood, becoming Ottoman Empire province (sanjak). Last Despot Lazar Branković fled to Hungarian exile. Serbian nobility destroyed or exiled, land replaced by Ottoman feudal system. Orthodox Church suppressed but allowed to continue existing. 1459 marked official end of medieval Serbian state, opening nearly four centuries of Ottoman rule. This year symbolizes freedom loss and beginning of "Turkish yoke" in Serbian history, becoming traumatic moment in national memory.

events.title: Ottoman Rule Period
events.description: Serbia spent nearly 345 years under Ottoman Empire rule. Serbia organized into multiple sanjaks (administrative districts), later becoming part of Belgrade Pashalik. Ottomans introduced timar feudal system, Islamic ruling class replaced Christian nobility. Many Serbs converted to Islam, especially in cities and Bosnia. Christians paid jizya (poll tax), status as dhimmi (protected people). Devşirme (blood tax) system conscripted Christian boys into Ottoman army (Janissaries) or administration. Orthodox Church maintained presence in Peć Patriarchate, becoming fortress of national identity. Monasteries preserved cultural heritage and national memory. Serbian population migrated north, fleeing to Habsburg territories ("Great Migrations"). Ottoman rule had profound impact on Serbian society, culture and demographic distribution. Despite oppression, Serbian national identity preserved through Church, folk traditions and epic poetry.

events.title: Fall of Belgrade
events.description: Ottoman Sultan Suleiman I (the Magnificent) conquered Belgrade from Hungary after bloody siege. Belgrade was fortress resisting Ottoman expansion, its fall opened road to Central Europe. This conquest directly led to 1526 Battle of Mohács and Hungarian Kingdom's collapse. Belgrade under Ottoman rule became important border city and military center, called "Dar al-Harb House" (House of Holy War). City landscape changed, mosques, Turkish baths and oriental bazaars built. Belgrade would spend nearly two centuries under Ottoman rule, repeatedly becoming battlefield of Austrian-Ottoman wars.

events.title: Banat Uprising
events.description: Serbs launched major uprising in Banat region encouraged by Austria, rebelling against Ottoman rule. Uprising led by Bishop Teodor, supported by Habsburg Empire, hoping to exploit Ottoman difficulties in Long Turkish War (1593-1606). Uprising brutally suppressed by Ottomans. In retaliation, Ottomans burned Saint Sava's relics in Belgrade, enormous desecration and trauma for Serbs. Relic burning day (May 27) became important Serbian Orthodox commemoration. This uprising and suppression deepened Serbian hatred of Ottoman rule, inspiring future generations' resistance spirit. After uprising failed, many Serbs fled to Habsburg territories, beginning large-scale northward migration.

events.title: Great Serbian Migration
events.description: During Great Turkish War (1683-1699), approximately 30,000-40,000 Serbian families migrated from Kosovo and southern Serbia to Habsburg Austria under Patriarch Arsenije III's leadership. Serbs supported Austria against Ottomans, but faced Ottoman retaliation when Austrian armies withdrew. Great Migration changed Balkan demographic map: Kosovo's Serbian population decreased, Albanians gradually became majority. Serbs migrating north settled in Vojvodina, Slavonia and Military Frontier. Austrian Emperor granted Serbs privileges (Privilegia), including religious freedom, autonomy and land in Military Frontier, in exchange for border defense service. Great Migration was major event in Serbian history, followed by Second Great Migration in 1737. Northern Serbian communities became centers of 18th-19th century national revival.

events.title: Treaty of Passarowitz
events.description: Ottoman Empire and Habsburg Empire signed Treaty of Passarowitz, ending 1716-1718 war. Austria gained northern Serbia including Belgrade, plus Banat and Oltenia. This marked end of Ottoman expansion in Europe and beginning of retreat. During 1718-1739, Belgrade and northern Serbia under Austrian rule experienced brief westernization and modernization: defensive fortifications built, Austrian administration introduced, economic development. But after 1739 Treaty of Belgrade, these territories returned to Ottomans. Brief Austrian rule let Serbs experience Western institutions, strengthening dissatisfaction with Ottoman rule. Treaty of Passarowitz marked shift in Balkan power balance, Ottoman Empire entering decline period.

events.title: Koča's Frontier Uprising
events.description: During Austro-Ottoman War (1787-1791), Serbs launched uprising under Koča (Koča Anđelković) leadership, establishing short-lived rebel government controlling Šumadija region. Rebels established assembly (Skupština), organized self-government, cooperating with Austrian forces. This was early attempt at modern Serbian national liberation movement, showing Serbian desire for autonomy and statehood. But with 1791 Treaty of Sistova restoring pre-war status, Austria withdrew, uprising failed. Ottoman Dahije (Janissary officers) restored control, brutally retaliating against rebels. Koča uprising's failure and subsequent oppression directly led to 1804 First Serbian Uprising. This uprising was precursor to Serbian revolutionary movement, cultivating organizational experience and national consciousness.

events.title: First Serbian Uprising
events.description: Serbs launched uprising under Karađorđe Petrović ("Black George") leadership, rebelling against tyrannical Dahije rule of Belgrade Pashalik. Uprising's initial goal was overthrowing Dahije and restoring Sultan's legitimate rule, but quickly evolved into national liberation war fighting for complete independence. Rebels held assembly in Orašac, electing Karađorđe as supreme leader. Uprising achieved rapid success, liberating most of Šumadija region. 1806 rebels captured Belgrade. Serbia established revolutionary government, drafted constitution, built army and administration. Uprising received Russian Empire support, but after 1812 Russo-Turkish Treaty of Bucharest Russian support weakened. 1813 Ottoman massive counteroffensive crushed uprising, Karađorđe fled to Austria. Despite failure, First Uprising laid foundation for Serbian independence movement, inspiring subsequent revolutions.

events.title: Second Serbian Uprising
events.description: Under Ottoman suppression and terror rule, Serbs launched Second Uprising under Miloš Obrenović leadership. Unlike First Uprising's military nature, Miloš adopted more diplomatic and political strategy, seeking negotiation with Ottomans. Uprising quickly controlled Šumadija region. Miloš cleverly exploited Ottoman internal power struggles, reaching agreement with reformist Sultan Mahmud II. After 1815 uprising's military victory, Miloš began negotiating autonomy with Ottoman authorities. This uprising more successful than first, as it ultimately achieved partial goals through negotiation. Miloš became Serbia's de facto ruler, opening long process toward full autonomy. Second Uprising marked Serbian strategic shift from revolution to diplomacy.

events.title: Serbian Principality Autonomy
events.description: Ottoman Sultan Mahmud II issued Hatt-i Sharif decree, recognizing Serbia as autonomous principality with Miloš Obrenović as hereditary Prince. Serbia gained internal autonomy: own government, assembly (Skupština), tax system, but foreign affairs and defense still Ottoman-controlled, Serbia paid tribute to Sultan. Ottoman troops stationed in Belgrade and other fortresses. This was beginning of modern Serbian state-building. 1830 viewed as first step toward Serbian independence, though full independence came in 1878. Miloš began modernization reforms, establishing administration, education, economic systems. Autonomous status further confirmed and expanded in 1833 and 1838. Serbian Principality became model and hope for other Balkan national liberation movements.

events.title: Sretenje Constitution
events.description: Serbia promulgated Balkans' first constitution, called Sretenje Constitution, announced on Candlemas Day (Sretenje). Constitution drafted by Dimitrije Davidović, introducing modern principles like parliamentary democracy, separation of powers, civil rights, limiting Prince's power. This was one of Europe's most liberal constitutions, even more progressive than many Western European countries. But autocratic Prince Miloš and conservative nobles opposed constitution, Ottoman and Russia also pressured. Constitution implemented only few weeks before abolished, 1838 replaced by more conservative "Turkish Constitution" strengthening Prince's power and establishing oligarchy. Despite short-lived, Sretenje Constitution has symbolic significance in Serbian constitutional history, embodying liberalism and democratic ideals, inspiring later reformers.

events.title: Establishment of Belgrade Higher School
events.description: Prince Mihailo Obrenović III established Higher School (Velika škola) in Belgrade, beginning of Serbian higher education. School initially had philosophy, law and engineering departments, teaching in Serbian language, revolutionary for Balkans at that time. Higher School cultivated Serbia's modern intellectual class, bureaucrats and professionals, becoming engine of national renaissance and modernization. Many famous Serbian writers, scientists and politicians studied or taught here. 1905 Higher School upgraded to University of Belgrade, becoming one of Balkans' most important academic institutions. Educational development was key factor in Serbia's transformation from agricultural society to modern nation-state.

events.title: Garašanin's Načertanije Program
events.description: Serbian Interior Minister Ilija Garašanin drafted secret foreign policy document "Načertanije" ("Outline"), proposing Serbia should become core of South Slav unification in Balkans, restoring medieval Serbian Empire glory. Program advocated Serbia leading liberation and unification of Bosnia, Montenegro, Vojvodina, establishing "Greater Serbia." This idea influenced Serbian 19th-20th century foreign policy and nationalist movements, becoming ideological foundation of Yugoslav unification movement. Načertanije embodied Serbian expansionist ambitions but also reflected Balkan nationalism and unification complexity. This program later sparked controversy in Yugoslav Kingdom and wars, criticized as source of Greater Serbian hegemony.

events.title: Serbian National Romantic Cultural Revival
events.description: Mid-19th century Serbia experienced cultural and national revival, called Serbian Romanticism period. Poets, writers and scholars promoted national literature and language development. Vuk Stefanović Karadžić reformed Serbian language, created modern Serbian grammar and spelling, collected folk epics and songs, preserving oral tradition. His principle "write as you speak, read as written" revolutionized writing. Petar II Petrović-Njegoš created epic "Mountain Wreath" (Gorski vijenac), becoming Serbian literary masterpiece. Other writers like Branko Radičević promoted poetry modernization. This period laid foundation of Serbian modern national culture, synchronized with European Romantic nationalist trends.

events.title: Ottoman Troops Withdrawal
events.description: Through Prince Mihailo Obrenović III's diplomatic efforts, Ottoman troops finally withdrew from all Serbian fortresses including Belgrade Fortress. This was key moment of Serbia's de facto independence, though legally still Ottoman vassal. Withdrawal eliminated Ottoman's last physical presence in Serbia, Serbia gained complete territorial control. Mihailo began more ambitious modernization and military preparations, planning alliance with other Balkan states against Ottomans. Belgrade Fortress handover was moment of national celebration. Serbia began independent foreign policy, established standing army, developed industry and infrastructure. Ottoman withdrawal marked decisive step from autonomy toward full independence.

events.title: Serbian-Ottoman War and Independence
events.description: Serbia and Montenegro declared war on Ottoman Empire, supporting Bosnian and Bulgarian uprisings. War initially Serbian defeat, but Russian Empire intervened (1877-1878 Russo-Turkish War), defeating Ottomans. 1878 Treaty of San Stefano and Congress of Berlin recognized Serbia, Montenegro and Romania complete independence. Serbia gained territorial expansion, extending south to Niš and Vranje regions. This was Serbian history milestone: after nearly 400 years Ottoman rule and 74 years fighting for autonomy and independence, Serbia finally became fully sovereign state with international recognition. July 13, 1878 Congress of Berlin formally recognized Serbian independence. Prince Milan Obrenović's status confirmed, 1882 he elevated to King. Serbian independence was important victory for Balkan national liberation, but also marked beginning of new territorial and ethnic conflicts.

events.title: Kingdom of Serbia Proclaimed
events.description: Milan Obrenović elevated principality to kingdom, crowned as Serbian King Milan I. Kingdom proclamation marked Serbia's further elevation and prestige increase, equal with other European monarchies. New constitution established constitutional monarchy, though King retained considerable power. Belgrade as kingdom capital began rapid modernization, building European-style architecture, boulevards and institutions. Serbian Kingdom period experienced economic development, education expansion and cultural flourishing. However politically turbulent: Radical Party, Liberal Party competing, parliament conflicted with King, struggle between Obrenović and Karađorđević dynasties continued. Kingdom also faced diplomatic challenges: tensions with Austria-Hungary, territorial disputes with Bulgaria, claims on Bosnia.

events.title: First Railway Completed
events.description: Serbia's first railway line completed, connecting Belgrade with Niš, later extended to borders. Railway construction was important symbol of Serbian modernization, promoting economic development, trade and population mobility. Railway connected Serbia with European railway network, through Austria-Hungary to Vienna, through Ottoman Empire to Istanbul. Orient Express began passing through Serbia, Belgrade became transportation hub between East and West Europe. Railway also had strategic military significance, enhancing Serbia's mobilization capacity. Railway engineering contracted by foreign companies, Serbia incurred huge debts, leading to economic dependence. However railway undoubtedly accelerated Serbia's industrialization and urbanization process.

events.title: May Coup
events.description: Officers organization "Black Hand" launched bloody coup, assassinating unpopular King Alexander Obrenović and Queen Draga, ending Obrenović dynasty. Coup extremely brutal: royal couple shot and hacked in palace, bodies thrown out window. Petar Karađorđević (Peter I) elected new King, restoring Karađorđević dynasty. May Coup shocked Europe, Serbia temporarily internationally isolated. But after coup Serbia turned to more democratic and parliamentary governance, 1903 Constitution viewed as progressive document. New regime turned to pro-Russian and anti-Austrian policy, intensifying tensions with Austria-Hungary. Post-coup officer corps (especially Black Hand) gained enormous political influence, sowing seeds for future conflicts including 1914 Sarajevo assassination.

events.title: Pig War and Customs Conflict
events.description: Economic conflict between Serbia and Austria-Hungary, Austria trying to force Serbian economic and political submission through tariff sanctions. Austria banned Serbian pork imports (Serbia's main export), causing "Pig War." Serbia successfully found new markets (France, Germany), achieving economic diversification, reducing Austrian dependence. This tariff war strengthened Serbian nationalism and anti-Austrian sentiment, proving Serbian economic resilience. Pig War was important factor in pre-WWI Austro-Serbian relations deterioration, showing limits of imperialist economic coercion. Serbian victory increased national confidence, but also deepened Austria-Hungary's hostility, viewing it as threat to Balkan order.

events.title: Balkan Wars
events.description: Serbia joined Balkan League (Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece, Montenegro) against Ottoman Empire, First Balkan War (1912-1913) league victory. Serbia recovered Kosovo, Macedonian Vardar valley, territory almost doubled. But Second Balkan War (1913) Serbia, Greece, Romania and Ottoman united against Bulgaria, fighting for Macedonia. Serbia again victorious, consolidating control over northern Macedonia. Balkan Wars enabled Serbian territorial and population expansion, rising from small state to major Balkan power. But this intensified Austria-Hungary's fears, as powerful Serbia posed attraction and threat to its South Slav provinces (Bosnia, Croatia, Slovenia). Serbia sought Adriatic Sea access but blocked by Austria, deepening hostility. Balkan Wars paved way for WWI.

events.title: World War I
events.description: Serbia suffered enormously in WWI. War's early phase, Serbian army heroically resisted Austro-Hungarian invasion, winning Battle of Cer (August 1914) and Battle of Kolubara (December 1914), repelling invaders. But 1915 combined German, Austro-Hungarian and Bulgarian offensive overwhelmed Serbia. Serbian army and government conducted epic "Albanian Golgotha" retreat, crossing Albanian mountains in harsh winter fleeing to Adriatic Sea, tens of thousands died from hunger, disease and cold. Survivors evacuated by Allied navies to Greek Corfu Island, reorganized and continued fighting on Salonika Front. Serbian homeland occupied, people suffered oppression, famine and disease, estimated losses quarter to third of population (approximately 700,000-1,200,000 people). 1918 Serbian army broke through Salonika Front, liberating homeland. Serbia was WWI's most devastated country by population proportion, but as victor paved way for Yugoslav unification.

events.title: Sarajevo Assassination
events.description: Bosnian Serb youth Gavrilo Princip assassinated Austro-Hungarian Archduke Franz Ferdinand and wife Sophie in Sarajevo. Princip belonged to "Young Bosnia" movement, linked with Serbian secret military organization "Black Hand." Assassination on June 28 (Kosovo Battle anniversary) had symbolic significance. This assassination became WWI trigger. Austria-Hungary issued ultimatum to Serbia with harsh demands. Serbia accepted most terms but reserved partial sovereignty, Austria still declared war July 28. Alliance system (Triple Alliance vs Triple Entente) rapidly escalated regional conflict into world war. Sarajevo assassination was one of 20th century's most important historical moments, changing world course, leading to four empire collapses and tens of millions deaths.

events.title: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes Formed
events.description: After WWI, Serbian Kingdom unified with former Austro-Hungarian South Slav territories (Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, Vojvodina) and Montenegro, forming "Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes" (SHS Kingdom). Serbian dynasty's Peter I became unified state's king. This realized 19th century Yugoslav unification dream. New state's territory and population greatly increased, becoming Balkans' largest state. But unification problematic from start: ethnic tensions between Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, centralism vs federalism debate, Serbian dominance causing other ethnicities' resentment. Whether unification was victory or beginning of future disaster, historians still debate.

events.title: King Alexander's Dictatorship and Renaming 'Yugoslavia'
events.description: Facing parliamentary deadlock and worsening ethnic conflicts, King Aleksandar I abolished constitution, established royal dictatorship, banned political parties, imposed personal rule. October 3 same year, state officially renamed "Kingdom of Yugoslavia" ("Yugoslavia" meaning "Land of South Slavs"). Alexander tried unifying state through "Yugoslavism" ideology, emphasizing common Yugoslav identity rather than separate Serbian, Croatian identities. He reorganized administrative divisions, eliminating historical provincial boundaries, establishing nine non-ethnically divided provinces (banovinas). Dictatorship suppressed democracy but didn't solve ethnic problems, instead deepened Croatian and other ethnicities' resentment and separatist sentiment. Alexander's "integralism" viewed by many as another form of Serbian hegemony.

events.title: Assassination of King Alexander
events.description: King Aleksandar I assassinated during state visit to Marseille, France, by VMRO (Macedonian Revolutionary Organization) member conspiring with Croatian extremist organization "Ustaša." Assassination conducted publicly, filmed, becoming history's first recorded political assassination. Alexander's death plunged Yugoslavia into crisis. His son Peter II only 11 years old, Prince Paul became regent. Paul's regency tried compromising on ethnic issues, 1939 reached agreement with Croatia (Sporazum), establishing Croatian autonomous banovina. But this concession angered Serbian nationalists, didn't thoroughly solve problems. Alexander's assassination showed Yugoslav internal division depth and violence potential, foreshadowing WWII genocide and civil war.

events.title: WWII Occupation and Resistance
events.description: Serbia suffered brutal occupation and civil war in WWII. German occupation authorities brutally retaliated against any resistance, executing 100 civilians for 1 German soldier ratio. Serbian Jews almost entirely exterminated, approximately 90% perished. Two main resistance movements: royalist Chetniks led by Draža Mihailović and Communist Partisans led by Josip Broz Tito. Both factions not only fought occupiers but fought each other. Ustaša in Croatia committed genocide against Serbs, Jasenovac concentration camp became Serbian traumatic memory. Serbian villages burned, population died massively from combat, massacres, famine and disease. Tito's Partisans ultimately victorious, October 1944 with Soviet Red Army liberated Belgrade. Serbia lost approximately 700,000 in WWII. War trauma and ethnic hatreds would cast shadows for decades.

events.title: March Coup
events.description: Serbian Air Force General Dušan Simović led coup, overthrowing regency government that signed Tripartite Pact with Nazi Germany. Coup had widespread popular support, Belgrade erupted in mass anti-German demonstrations, slogans "Better war than pact" (Bolje rat nego pakt) and "Better grave than slave" (Bolje grob nego rob). Young King Peter II declared of age, personally ruled. Coup enraged Hitler, he ordered "merciless destruction" of Yugoslavia. Only two weeks later, Germany and Axis invaded Yugoslavia. March Coup viewed as Serbian heroic moment resisting Nazis, embodying national honor and refusal to submit spirit. But it also directly led to Yugoslav invasion and subsequent brutal occupation, civil war and genocide.

events.title: Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia Established
events.description: Tito's Communists proclaimed Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia, monarchy abolished, King Peter II exiled. New Yugoslavia was federal socialist state, composed of six republics: Serbia, Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Macedonia and Montenegro, plus two autonomous provinces within Serbia: Vojvodina and Kosovo. Tito became lifelong leader, establishing Communist one-party dictatorship. Federation aimed balancing ethnicities, suppressing nationalism with "Brotherhood and Unity" (bratstvo i jedinstvo) slogan. But Serbia considered relatively weakened under new system: largest republic divided into three parts (Serbia proper + two autonomous provinces), while other republics remained intact. This asymmetric structure sowed seeds for future conflicts. Yugoslavia began socialist construction, industrialization and modernization, but at cost of harsh political repression.

events.title: Tito-Stalin Split
events.description: Tito-led Yugoslavia broke with Soviet Union and Cominform (Communist International). Stalin wanted controlling Yugoslavia, but Tito refused Moscow submission, insisting independent socialist path. Soviet Union and Eastern European satellites imposed economic and diplomatic blockade on Yugoslavia, even threatened military invasion. Yugoslavia expelled from Cominform, faced isolation. But Tito successfully resisted pressure, Yugoslavia turned to non-aligned policy, establishing economic relations with West while maintaining socialist system. Split made Tito unique figure between East and West, strengthening his domestic authority and international prestige. Yugoslavia developed "self-management socialism" model, different from Soviet model. Tito-Stalin split proved small state's possibility of resisting superpower pressure, giving Yugoslavia special Cold War status.

events.title: Yugoslav Golden Age and Non-Aligned Movement
events.description: Titoist Yugoslavia experienced rapid economic development and relative prosperity. Industrialization, urbanization accelerated, living standards improved, Yugoslavia became one of wealthiest socialist states. Introduced worker self-management system, enterprises managed by worker councils, different from Soviet central planning. Yugoslav citizens enjoyed relatively free travel rights, could work in Western countries. Tito played important international role, with Egypt's Nasser and India's Nehru co-founded Non-Aligned Movement (1961), representing Third World countries unwilling to join East-West camps. Belgrade became important Non-Aligned Movement center. Yugoslavia enjoyed international prestige and influence far exceeding actual power. Culture and arts relatively free, Yugoslav films, music gained international recognition. This was "Yugoslav Dream" peak period.

events.title: Ranković Affair
events.description: Tito purged Vice President and security chief Aleksandar Ranković, a Serbian hardliner. Ranković accused of abusing secret police power, including bugging Tito himself, and oppressing Kosovo Albanians. His downfall viewed as weakening Serbian influence in federation. After Ranković's fall, Yugoslavia began decentralization reforms, republics gained more autonomy. Kosovo Albanians' status improved, later Kosovo gained greater autonomy. Many Serbs viewed Ranković Affair as Tito's strategy weakening Serbia, believing security apparatus purge deprived Serbia of last power lever in federation. This event sowed seeds of Serbian nationalist resentment, impacting profoundly into 1980s-1990s.

events.title: 1974 Constitution
events.description: Yugoslavia promulgated new constitution, massively decentralizing, granting six republics and two autonomous provinces (Vojvodina and Kosovo) powers almost equal to republics. Kosovo and Vojvodina gained own parliaments, courts, constitutions and veto powers, though nominally still belonging to Serbian Republic. Federation became loose confederation, central government power greatly weakened. Collective presidency replaced personal leadership, preparing for post-Tito transition. 1974 Constitution caused enormous Serbian resentment, many believing it weakened Serbia: two autonomous provinces effectively separated from Serbia, while Serbia proper lacked corresponding representation and powers. Constitution considered mechanism preventing Serbian federation dominance. This resentment erupted in 1980s, becoming important factor in Yugoslav disintegration. Critics called 1974 Constitution time bomb for state fragmentation.

events.title: Death of Tito
events.description: Josip Broz Tito died age 87, ruling Yugoslavia 35 years. His death marked era's end. Entire Yugoslavia and international community mourned, funeral attracted leaders worldwide. Tito viewed as Yugoslav unity symbol and guarantee, his personal authority suppressed ethnic contradictions. After Tito's death, Yugoslavia implemented collective leadership: eight-member presidency (six republics + two autonomous provinces, one each) rotating chairmanship. But without Tito's strong leadership, ethnic contradictions and economic problems gradually emerged. Famous prophecy "After Tito, chaos" began materializing. 1980s Yugoslavia fell into economic crisis, inflation and political deadlock. Ten years after Tito's death, Yugoslavia began disintegrating, bloody wars followed. His legacy still sparks intense debate in former Yugoslav regions.

events.title: Kosovo Albanian Demonstrations
events.description: Kosovo Albanians (approximately 80% of Kosovo population) erupted in mass demonstrations, demanding Kosovo elevation from autonomous province to full republic, equal with Serbia. Demonstrations quickly evolved into violent clashes, Yugoslavia sent troops and police to suppress. Hundreds arrested, several killed. Serbs viewed these demonstrations as separatist threat, believing Albanians trying to separate Kosovo from Serbia or even merge with Albania. Serbian media reported Kosovo Serbs suffering discrimination and pressure, forced to migrate out, though these reports' accuracy disputed. 1981 events marked Kosovo problem outbreak, becoming core issue in 1980s-1990s Serbian politics. Kosovo, sacred land in Serbian national mythology, became focus of nationalist mobilization and future conflict flashpoint.

events.title: SANU Memorandum
events.description: Group of intellectuals from Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts (SANU) drafted memorandum, claiming Serbs unjustly treated and discriminated in Yugoslav federation. Memorandum criticized 1974 Constitution weakening Serbia, accused Kosovo Albanians of "ethnic cleansing" against Serbs, calling for protecting Serbian national interests. Memorandum stirred Serbian nationalist sentiment, becoming ideological manifesto of Serbian national revival movement. Though criticized by Titoists at time, memorandum's views rapidly spread among Serbian population. It paved way for Slobodan Milošević's rise and nationalist politics. Critics considered memorandum blueprint for Greater Serbian nationalism, fueling nationalist wave leading to Yugoslav disintegration and wars. SANU Memorandum is key document for understanding 1990s Balkan tragedy.

events.title: Milošević's Rise at Kosovo Polje
events.description: Serbian Communist leader Slobodan Milošević visited Kosovo Polje, meeting local Serbs. When Serbs clashed with Albanian police, Milošević told crowd famous words: "No one should dare to beat you!" (Niko ne sme da vas bije!) This phrase broadcast on TV, making Milošević overnight celebrity, becoming symbol of Serbian national hero and protector. Milošević exploited Kosovo issue to mobilize nationalism, consolidating power. He transformed from Titoist technocrat to nationalist politician, seizing Serbian discontent and fears. Kosovo Polje event marked Milošević's political rise turning point, he would dominate Serbian and Yugoslav politics over a decade, ultimately leading to catastrophic wars and state disintegration.

events.title: Kosovo Battle 600th Anniversary and Autonomy Revocation
events.description: Milošević held massive Kosovo Battle 600th anniversary commemoration at Kosovo Polje, reportedly million attendees. Milošević delivered incendiary speech, hinting Serbs might again face "battles," emphasizing ethnic unity and resistance. Same year, Milošević exploited nationalist pressure and political manipulation, forcing Kosovo and Vojvodina assemblies to vote abandoning autonomy, restoring Serbian central control. This violated 1974 Constitution, triggering alarm and opposition from other Yugoslav republics. Kosovo Albanians launched strikes and nonviolent resistance, establishing parallel institutions. Autonomy revocation was important Yugoslav disintegration catalyst: Slovenia and Croatia believed if Serbia could unilaterally change constitutional arrangements, they needed seeking independence protection. 1989 marked Yugoslav path to disintegration's crucial year.

events.title: Multi-party System and Milošević Elected
events.description: Yugoslav republics introduced multi-party democracy, holding first free elections. Serbia held elections December 1990, Milošević's Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS, reorganized Communist Party) won victory, Milošević became Serbian President. Opposition fragmented, Milošević controlled media, exploited nationalist sentiment to consolidate power. Same year, Serbia promulgated new constitution, formally reducing Kosovo and Vojvodina autonomous status. Meanwhile, Slovenia and Croatia elected pro-independence governments. Kosovo Albanians declared independence (unrecognized), establishing parallel republic. 1990 elections established nationalist governments in Yugoslav republics, laying political foundation for disintegration and conflict. Democratization in Yugoslav context became tool for ethnic mobilization and separation, rather than unifying force.

events.title: Yugoslav Disintegration Begins
events.description: Slovenia and Croatia declared independence, Yugoslavia officially began disintegrating. Yugoslav People's Army (JNA) intervened to prevent Slovenian independence, but after Ten-Day War withdrew, Slovenia achieved independence. Croatian independence triggered full-scale war with local Serbs (12% of Croatian population) and JNA. Serbian government supported Serbian rebellion in Croatia, establishing separatist entities like "Republic of Serbian Krajina." War rapidly escalated, Vukovar siege (November 1991) became brutal symbol, city destroyed, hundreds of civilians massacred. Yugoslav disintegration accompanied Europe's bloodiest conflict since WWII. Serbia accused by international community as aggressor, though Milošević claimed protecting Serbs. UN intervened, imposing sanctions on Serbia. Yugoslav dream ended in blood and fire.

events.title: Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Formed
events.description: After Slovenia, Croatia, Macedonia and Bosnia successively independent, Serbia and Montenegro declared forming "Federal Republic of Yugoslavia" (FRY), claiming to inherit original Yugoslavia. But international community refused recognizing it as sole successor state, requiring reapplication for UN membership. New Yugoslavia actually controlled by Milošević, Montenegro in subordinate position. Same year, Bosnian War erupted, becoming Yugoslav dissolution wars' bloodiest and most complex conflict. Bosnian Serbs (approximately 31% population) with Serbian and JNA support opposed independence, establishing "Republika Srpska." War lasted until 1995, causing approximately 100,000 deaths, 2 million displaced, including atrocities like Srebrenica genocide. Serbia suffered international isolation and severe sanctions for supporting Bosnian Serbs.

events.title: Dayton Agreement and Sanctions
events.description: US-led Dayton Peace Agreement ended Bosnian War. Milošević represented Bosnian Serbs in negotiations, viewed by West as peacemaker, though he previously supported war. Bosnia divided into two entities: Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina (Bosniaks and Croats) and Republika Srpska. International Criminal Tribunal for former Yugoslavia (ICTY) established in Hague, prosecuting war criminals including Bosnian Serb leaders Radovan Karadžić and Ratko Mladić. UN sanctions on Serbia gradually lifted after Dayton Agreement, but economy already devastated. 1990s Serbia experienced hyperinflation (1993 worst month inflation rate reached 313 million %), poverty, isolation and social collapse. A generation grew up in war, sanctions and nationalist propaganda. Serbian society deeply traumatized and polarized.

events.title: Mass Anti-Government Protests
events.description: November 1996 local elections, opposition alliance Zajedno ("Together") won in many cities including Belgrade, but Milošević regime tried canceling results. This triggered three months of mass protests, hundreds of thousands daily taking to streets. Protesters blew whistles, banged pots, Belgrade became "City of Whistles." Student movement played key role. International pressure and domestic protests forced Milošević to eventually recognize election results. This was 1990s largest anti-Milošević movement, showing civil society strength and democracy desire. But opposition subsequently fragmented, failed exploiting this victory. Milošević retained power, turning to more authoritarian tactics and media control. These protests were rehearsal for 2000 Milošević overthrow.

events.title: Kosovo War
events.description: Conflict between Kosovo Albanian armed organization Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) and Serbian security forces escalated to full war. Serbian police and army suppressed Albanian villages, causing massive civilian casualties and hundreds of thousands refugees. 1998 Račak massacre (45 Albanian civilians killed) shocked international community. Western countries demanded Serbia stop repression and accept Kosovo autonomy, but Milošević refused. March 1999, NATO began bombing Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro) without UN authorization, lasting 78 days. Bombing targets included military facilities, infrastructure and government buildings, causing approximately 500 civilian deaths, cities like Belgrade suffered severe destruction. June, Milošević forced to surrender, Serbian military and police withdrew from Kosovo, UN and NATO forces took over. Kosovo War was Milošević regime's final disaster, leading to its collapse one year later.

events.title: Democratic Revolution Overthrows Milošević
events.description: September 24, 2000 presidential election, opposition candidate Vojislav Koštunica defeated Milošević, but Milošević refused acknowledging defeat, announcing second round. October 5, hundreds of thousands from across country poured into Belgrade, demanding recognizing election results. Protesters stormed parliament and state television, symbolically seizing power, state TV RTS occupation marked end of Milošević propaganda machine. Police and military refused suppressing, revolution almost bloodless. That evening Milošević acknowledged defeat. October 5 called "Bulldozer Revolution," Serbian modern history turning point, ending Milošević's 13-year authoritarian rule. Koštunica became Yugoslav President (later Serbian President). Serbia began democratic transition and reconciliation with West, though process full of challenges and setbacks.

events.title: Milošević Arrested
events.description: Former President Slobodan Milošević arrested by Serbian police at Belgrade mansion after 40-hour standoff. He charged with corruption, abuse of power. June 28 (Kosovo Battle anniversary, symbolic choice), Milošević extradited to Hague ICTY, facing war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide charges. Extradition sparked controversy in Serbia, many opposed handing former leader to "foreign court," but reformist government considered this necessary step for reconciliation with international community. Milošević became first former head of state tried by international court. Trial lasted four years, March 2006 Milošević died in prison from heart attack, trial unfinished. His arrest and trial marked Serbian attempt breaking with past, but also revealed society's deep divisions over war and responsibility.

events.title: Prime Minister Zoran Đinđić Assassinated
events.description: Reform Prime Minister Zoran Đinđić assassinated outside Belgrade government building, gunman linked to organized crime groups and former security personnel. Đinđić was key figure in 2000 democratic revolution, promoting reforms, fighting organized crime and achieving Milošević's extradition. His assassination shocked Serbia and international community, exposing dangerous alliance of underworld, nationalist extremists and old regime remnants. Government declared state of emergency, arrested thousands, destroyed several criminal organizations including notorious "Zemun clan." Đinđić assassination was tragic moment in Serbian modern history, marking reform agenda setback. Many believe Serbia lost most capable reformer, subsequent governments more cautious and compromising. Đinđić became martyr of Serbian democratic transition, but his legacy remains controversial.

events.title: Montenegro Independence and Serbia-Montenegro Dissolution
events.description: Montenegro held independence referendum, 55.5% voted for independence, just exceeding EU-set 55% threshold. June 3 Montenegro officially declared independence, June 5 Serbian Parliament declared Serbia as successor state to Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This marked Yugoslavia's final dissolution: state established 1918 completely ended. Serbia became independent state, losing last "Yugoslav" label. Montenegro independence peacefully conducted, contrasting with 1990s bloody separations. Serbian society reacted complexly to Montenegro independence: some grieved losing brother nation, others considered this opportunity shedding burden. After independence Serbia began redefining national identity, no longer multi-ethnic federation core, but single nation-state (though still with minorities). Kosovo issue became more pressing matter.

events.title: Kosovo Unilateral Independence Declaration
events.description: Kosovo Assembly unilaterally declared independence from Serbia, gaining US and most EU states recognition. Serbia refused recognizing, calling independence illegal and violating international law (UN Security Council Resolution 1244 and Serbian Constitution). Serbia launched diplomatic campaign preventing Kosovo from gaining more recognition, sought International Court of Justice ruling on independence legality (2010 court ruled independence declaration itself didn't violate international law, but didn't judge whether independence was valid). Kosovo independence caused enormous anger and grief in Serbia, Belgrade protests erupted, US Embassy burned. All political factions refused recognizing Kosovo independence, this became Serbian politics red line and national consensus. Kosovo issue seriously obstructs Serbian relations with West and EU accession process. Serbia insists "Kosovo is Serbia" slogan, but hope of actually controlling Kosovo slim. By 2024 approximately 100 UN member states recognized Kosovo, including US and most EU countries, but Russia, China and five EU members refuse.

events.title: Radovan Karadžić Arrested
events.description: Bosnian Serb wartime leader Radovan Karadžić arrested in Belgrade after 13 years fugitive. Karadžić disguised as "alternative medicine" expert, growing long hair and beard, lived and worked in Belgrade for years undiscovered. He charged with genocide (including Srebrenica massacre of 8,000+ Bosniak Muslim men and boys), war crimes and crimes against humanity. Karadžić extradited to Hague tribunal, 2016 sentenced to 40 years imprisonment, 2019 appeal increased to life imprisonment. His arrest was important step in Serbian reckoning with past and EU accession process. But in Serbia, many still view Karadžić as national hero rather than war criminal, reflecting society's divisions over war memory. Karadžić case symbolizes challenges of dealing with war legacy.

events.title: Ratko Mladić Arrested
events.description: Former Bosnian Serb Army Commander Ratko Mladić arrested in northern Serbian village after 16 years fugitive. Mladić called "Butcher of Bosnia," accused of orchestrating Srebrenica genocide and Sarajevo siege (1992-1996, lasting 1,425 days, causing approximately 11,000 deaths including 1,500 children). He extradited to Hague, 2017 convicted of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity, sentenced to life imprisonment. Mladić's arrest completed hunt for major Yugoslav war criminals, Hague tribunal's work nearing end. But in Serbia, Mladić still has many supporters viewing him as military hero, his arrest and conviction sparked divisions in society. Different perceptions of war responsibility continue dividing Serbian society and obstructing regional reconciliation.

events.title: EU Candidate Status Granted
events.description: EU granted Serbia candidate status, recognizing Serbian reform efforts and European integration process. This was important achievement in Serbian post-2000 foreign policy, marking path from 1990s isolation toward European integration. Candidate status is formal step toward EU membership, though actual accession still requires years of negotiations and reforms. 2014 Serbia began formal EU accession negotiations. But EU accession process slow and complex due to Kosovo issue, rule of law reforms, media freedom, reckoning with war past. Serbia needs achieving relations normalization with Kosovo as accession condition, but this domestically very unpopular. Meanwhile, Serbia maintains close relations with Russia and China, trying balancing between East and West, sometimes conflicting with EU expectations. EU prospect is driver of Serbian modernization, but process full of political challenges.

events.title: Belgrade-Pristina Dialogue
events.description: Under EU mediation, Serbia and Kosovo began relations normalization dialogue. April 2013 reached "Brussels Agreement" concerning Kosovo northern Serb region integration. Serbia agreed not obstructing Kosovo membership in international organizations, in exchange for Kosovo northern Serb community autonomy and protection. But agreement implementation difficult, parties interpret agreement differently, mutual distrust persists. 2015 Serbia and Kosovo signed multiple technical agreements under EU facilitation (energy, telecommunications, license plates), but political core issue (mutual recognition) unresolved. Dialogue process repeatedly stalled, both sides exploit each other as domestic political scapegoats. Serbia insists not recognizing Kosovo sovereignty, proposing controversial "compromise solutions" and "land swap." Kosovo demands full recognition. Dialogue is key condition for Serbian EU accession, but prospects for final agreement unclear.

events.title: Aleksandar Vučić Elected President
events.description: Former Serbian Radical Party member, later turned pro-European stance Aleksandar Vučić elected Serbian President, previously serving as Prime Minister since 2014. Vučić dominates Serbian politics to this day, his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) controls parliament. Vučić promoted economic reforms, attracting foreign investment (especially from China and UAE), infrastructure construction, Serbian economy achieved growth in 2010s. But he also criticized for concentrating power, controlling media, weakening democratic institutions and rule of law. Opposition and civil society accuse Vučić of establishing "soft authoritarian" regime, manipulating elections and suppressing dissent. International organizations expressed concerns about Serbian media freedom deterioration, judicial independence and corruption. Vučić diplomatically tries balancing between EU, Russia, China and US, sometimes called "multi-vector" policy. He enjoys high domestic approval ratings, but critics argue this results from media manipulation and lack of genuine alternatives.

events.title: 1 of 5 Million Protest Movement
events.description: Mass anti-government protests erupted in Belgrade and other cities, opposing Vučić government's authoritarianism, media control and corruption. Protest movement named "One of Five Minutes for One Ballot," later changed to "1 of 5 Million," implying even if 5 million people (Vučić's claimed supporter number) oppose, they would continue protesting. Protests held every Saturday, lasting months, attracting tens of thousands. Demonstrators demanded media freedom, fair elections and Vučić's resignation. But protests failed shaking government, opposition fragmented and unable to unite. Government-controlled media belittled or ignored protests. Protests eventually weakened, Vučić consolidated power. This movement showed civil society vitality and democracy desire, but also exposed challenges opposition faces in environment with media unfreedom and manipulated political system.

events.title: COVID Pandemic and Washington Agreement
events.description: Serbia affected by COVID pandemic, Vučić government's response criticized, especially post-election admission of pandemic severity accused as political manipulation. During pandemic Serbia received Chinese vaccine assistance, Vučić kissed Chinese flag expressing gratitude, strengthening China relations. September 2020, under Trump administration mediation, Serbia and Kosovo signed economic normalization agreement in Washington ("Washington Agreement" or "Abraham Accords Balkans version"). Agreement focused on economic cooperation (railways, highways), but sparked controversy: Kosovo agreed pausing seeking international recognition for one year, Serbia agreed moving embassy to Jerusalem (later not executed), involved Israel relations normalization. Agreement criticized as US pre-election PR, didn't solve core political issues. Subsequent implementation limited, but marked US re-engagement in Balkan affairs.

events.title: Serbia's Stance in Russia-Ukraine War and Kosovo Tensions
events.description: After 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, Serbia in difficult diplomatic position. Serbia voted at UN condemning Russian invasion, but refused joining Western sanctions against Russia, emphasizing "brotherly relations" with Russia and energy dependence. Vučić tries balancing West and Russia, but faces pressure. Meanwhile, Kosovo northern Serb region tensions escalated: 2022-2023 license plate and ID disputes, Serb boycott of Kosovo institutions, armed clashes. May 2023 Kosovo police entering Serb municipal halls triggered violence, NATO peacekeepers clashed with Serb demonstrators, 30 soldiers injured. Serbian military massed at border, regional tensions reached multi-year high. International community worried about new conflict. EU and US pressured both sides to de-escalate. By 2024, Serbia continues struggling balancing EU integration, Russia relations, Kosovo issue and domestic democracy, future direction still uncertain. Serbia is complex Balkan crossroads, history's heavy legacy, prospects full of challenges.
